title: Trial Presentation Software: 7 Options for Courtroom Work
summary: Compare seven trial presentation software options by platform, evidence handling, pricing, operator fit, and courtroom reliability for hearings and trials.
body_markdown:
Trial presentation software has a simple assignment: put the right evidence or court-approved visual on the right screen immediately while keeping the operator's working view private. The difficult part is choosing around the case, operator, and courtroom instead of buying from a feature list. A useful comparison starts with document and video demands, then accounts for external displays, offline access, training, and failure recovery.


## What trial presentation software must do


Also called courtroom or evidence presentation software, this category organizes and displays documents, photographs, audio, video, deposition clips, and demonstratives during a hearing or trial. Unlike an ordinary slide deck, it can retrieve an unplanned exhibit, zoom into a passage, compare two documents, annotate evidence live, and keep menus or private notes off the audience display.


Five capabilities determine whether a product will hold up in court:


- **Immediate retrieval:** The operator needs a stable naming convention, full-text search, witness folders, and shortcuts that make an exhibit available within seconds.
- **Controlled output:** A blank, freeze, preview, or on-air control keeps the jury from watching the operator search. Independent controls separate the operator and presentation displays.
- **Evidence handling:** The software must support the actual mix of searchable PDFs, images, native video, synchronized deposition testimony, audio, and demonstratives in the matter.
- **Local resilience:** Core presentation functions should remain available when courthouse Wi-Fi is slow or unavailable. Local copies of case files reduce dependence on network access.
- **Recoverability:** A second machine, duplicate case data, common-format exports, spare adapters, and a written fallback sequence turn a technical failure into a short pause.


Courtroom compatibility belongs in the buying decision. Court facilities vary by room, judge, and district. The Northern District of California tells counsel to bring backup presentation equipment, convert specialized evidence to compatible formats, and become familiar with the equipment before court. Its[courtroom technology guidance](https://cand.uscourts.gov/attorneys/courtroom-technology) also shows why a single laptop setup cannot be assumed to work everywhere: some rooms use HDMI, others still specify VGA and 1024 x 768 output.


## Trial presentation software compared


The right option follows the matter's operator, evidence mix, hardware, and proceeding. These seven products are organized by their clearest use case, without a universal rank.


This is a desk-researched comparison based on public vendor and court materials, not hands-on product testing. Prices and plan details were checked on October 5, 2026; confirm them before purchase. The screenshots are September 2026 captures of each vendor's public website. The use-case recommendations are our assessment of the listed capabilities.

Pricing is only one part of cost. Training, deposition synchronization, trial-tech support, extra activations, storage, case migration, and a duplicate presentation machine can exceed the license difference.


### OnCue: for an operator-led, video-heavy trial


OnCue is purpose-built for live courtroom control on Windows. It fits a record with extensive deposition designations, multimedia, many exhibits, and a trained person in the hot seat. The software includes saved workspace layouts, exhibit search, independent display control, On-Air Mode, video editing, scrolling transcript text, and designation timing.


The[OnCue pricing page](https://www.oncuetech.com/plans) lists Flex at $100 per month for two activations. Pro is $900 per year for two activations and includes one ProSync job per month. OnCue stores case data locally rather than providing cloud storage, which is helpful in court but makes the team's copy and backup discipline important.


OnCue asks more of the operator than an iPad-first tool. That tradeoff is sensible when the matter needs live video edits, designation management, and fast retrieval across a large database. A short hearing with a small, fully scripted exhibit set may not use that depth.


### TrialPad: for attorney-controlled presentation on Mac or iPad


TrialPad gives a lawyer or paralegal a direct way to organize, annotate, and present evidence from an iPad or Mac. It can display documents and multimedia, create callouts and highlights, compare two items in split view, edit video clips, and use Blank, Freeze, and Present controls for the external screen. Private presenter notes stay in the working view.


TrialPad comes only through LIT SUITE. The[LIT SUITE subscription](https://app.litsoftware.com/) costs $600 annually and includes TrialPad, TranscriptPad, DocReviewPad, TimelinePad, and ExhibitsPad across three compatible Apple devices, with a seven-day trial. The bundle has more value when the team will also review transcripts, prepare documents, or build timelines. Teams that need only a few hours of exhibit display still pay for the full suite.


File preparation matters.[LIT SOFTWARE’s supported-file guidance](https://support.litsoftware.com/supported-file-types-in-lit-suite) recommends PDF for documents and supports common image, video, and audio formats, but it does not present native Word, Excel, or PowerPoint files. Those materials need to enter the case in a supported format.


### ExhibitView Trial Presenter: for dedicated Windows presentation


ExhibitView Trial Presenter covers the core courtroom jobs: witness and hot-document folders, exhibit search, live annotation, side-by-side display, web content, and synchronized deposition playback. Its controls serve attorneys, paralegals, prosecutors, and litigation-support teams that want dedicated presentation and synchronized-video functions in the same Windows application.


The product page lists a $670.88 buy-now price and a five-day trial. ExhibitView's desktop products run on Windows. Its iTrial companion provides an iPad presentation route, and TranscriptPro handles deeper transcript work.


[ExhibitView’s support materials](https://exhibitview.net/faqs/) identify display scaling as a source of misplaced annotations. The courtroom machine should use the same display scaling, cables, and output arrangement as the final rehearsal. The vendor also recommends a backup computer and independent copies of the case.


### Case Crafter: for timeline-led stories across Windows, Mac, and iPad


Case Crafter combines case review, full-text document search, an interactive chronology, and direct presentation. Evidence can be attached to timeline events, then called up while the lawyer walks the fact finder through the sequence. The same case format moves among Windows, Mac, and iPad, and case data can remain local for offline presentation.


[Case Crafter’s pricing page](https://casecrafter.com/pricing/) lists Basic at $599 per user per year for up to 10 cloud cases, Pro at $749 for 25 cloud cases, and Unlimited at $899. These limits apply to cloud cases; local cases do not count toward them. Each plan includes cloud sync, team sharing, direct presentation, and a seven-day trial.[Downloaded cloud cases and local cases can be used offline](https://casecrafter.com/documentation/cases/cloud-cases/) .


The chronology-driven workflow fits a presentation organized around sequence and causation. A team focused on long synchronized deposition designations should compare its video workflow closely with OnCue, TRIAL DIRECTOR, ExhibitView, and Sanction. Case Crafter also spans Windows, Mac, and iPad in one case format.


### TRIAL DIRECTOR: for an established, complex Windows workflow


TRIAL DIRECTOR by Reveal manages documents, photographs, multimedia, transcripts, and digital video testimony in a case database. Its Presentation module supports keyboard and script retrieval, multiple display zones, annotations, saved stages, exhibit admission tracking, and Mirror Mode. The operator can work in Presentation Preview while the audience sees a clean secondary display.


This depth suits a litigation-support team with an existing TRIAL DIRECTOR workflow, trained users, and complex evidence. It also brings a heavier technical footprint.[Reveal’s system requirements](https://docs.revealdata.com/trial-director/docs/system-requirements-trial-director) recommend a dedicated graphics card and 16 GB of memory for courtroom presentation and list Windows 10 and 11. Confirm the supported operating-system and hardware configuration for the version you will deploy.


Reveal’s public TRIAL DIRECTOR product page does not list a price; ask the vendor for a quote. The implementation budget should account for operator training, hardware, case migration, and the team's chosen deposition-sync process.


### Sanction: for evidence organization and multimedia on Windows


LexisNexis Sanction assembles documents, exhibits, transcripts, visuals, audio, and video in a Windows application. It can synchronize testimony with deposition video, play documents beside media, edit clips during trial, and apply bulk changes across a case file.


Sanction serves Windows-based teams that already work with CaseMap or want evidence preparation and live presentation under one vendor. It uses a traditional desktop deployment, so the firm's standard laptop build, media components, and screen arrangement belong in the rehearsal plan.


LexisNexis’s public product page offers a free trial and asks buyers to contact the vendor for pricing. The full deployment can include seats, training, support, and companion case-analysis tools.


### TrialView: for remote or hybrid proceedings


TrialView approaches presentation as one part of a cloud dispute workspace. It combines document bundles, cross-referencing, chronology work, evidence presentation across devices, video conferencing, and real-time transcription. Discrete screen controls separate the advocate's view from the public display.


This model fits an arbitration, tribunal, or hybrid hearing in which the participants already work through a shared digital bundle. Teams that require a local, offline workflow or a direct connection to a court evidence system should confirm TrialView’s connection, offline, and support options with the vendor and the court before selecting it.


TrialView’s public hearing-services page invites teams to contact the vendor rather than listing a price. Procurement should include the number of users and matters, storage, hearing services, transcription, data residency, export rights, and the offline fallback for the proceeding.


## Choose the operator before the software


Start by deciding who will run the presentation. A trial technician can exploit hotkeys, scripts, designation tools, multiple workspaces, and live edits without interrupting examination. A lawyer handling questions and evidence at the same time needs fewer controls, larger targets, and a predictable sequence.


The matter can change the answer. A self-operating attorney may use TrialPad for a short hearing and bring in a technician with OnCue for a multiweek jury trial.


Use these questions to narrow the shortlist:


1. **Who calls up exhibits?** Name the primary operator and backup operator before choosing an interface.
2. **How much is live and unscripted?** Cross-examination and rebuttal demand faster ad hoc retrieval than a fixed opening deck.
3. **Does the record depend on synchronized video?** Long designation lists, objections, scrolling text, and clip exchanges point toward deeper video tooling.
4. **Which devices will be in court?** Windows, Mac, and iPad support divides the market quickly.
5. **What may the audience see?** Preview, blank, freeze, and independent display controls protect privileged notes and prevent accidental display.
6. **What survives without internet access?** Local evidence and license behavior matter even when the courthouse offers Wi-Fi.


## Build a courtroom rehearsal around failure points


A successful software demo proves very little. The useful exercise uses the real case structure and the exact presentation path from operator input to courtroom screen.


The rehearsal should include:


- the primary and backup laptops, both running the complete case;
- every cable, adapter, charger, audio lead, clicker, and external drive that will enter the courtroom;
- ordinary PDFs, scanned exhibits, large documents, photographs, native video, deposition clips, audio, and any unusual codec;
- a scripted direct examination and an unscripted request for an exhibit, page, and callout;
- blanking the jury display while the operator searches or responds to an objection;
- recovery from a disconnected display, frozen application, missing file, failed audio route, and unusable primary machine;
- a common-format fallback set of critical exhibits and clips outside the presentation database.


Court procedures add their own timing. The Central District of California asks counsel to arrange an equipment session[one to three weeks ahead](https://www.cacd.uscourts.gov/clerk-services/courtroom-technology/presenting-evidence) , with a three-day minimum. The U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Massachusetts highly recommends that users of Apple or iOS devices arrange a compatibility test[at least a week ahead](https://www.mab.uscourts.gov/electronics-courtroom) . Those are local examples, but they capture the broader rule: software selection is incomplete until the full courtroom signal path has been rehearsed.


## Where we fit in a patent trial stack


We provide the upstream AI workspace for patent litigation. The products above are the live display layer. Patent teams use our workspace to search prior art, review source material, analyze invalidity and infringement, and build[source-grounded Claim Charts](https://www.tryandai.com/product/claim-charts) with limitation-level evidence and pinpoint citations. Attorneys review the mapping, control the content, and export the finished chart to Word.


The handoff to presentation software should be deliberate. A cited patent figure, specification passage, product document, claim-chart excerpt, or demonstrative becomes a controlled courtroom asset only after the team resolves admissibility, scope, and display format. This division keeps analysis and sources traceable in our workspace while the presentation tool handles retrieval, output screens, annotation, and playback.


For patent matters, the full stack usually needs both layers. Our[claim-chart workflow](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/submission-ready-claim-charts-with-ai) reduces the manual work of mapping limitations and assembling cited evidence. The selected presentation product then delivers the approved material in court.


## Frequently asked questions


### What is the best trial presentation software?


The best trial presentation software matches the operator and evidence. OnCue fits a trained operator handling complex video and exhibits. TrialPad fits an attorney presenting from a Mac or iPad. ExhibitView offers a dedicated Windows workflow, Case Crafter centers an interactive chronology, and TRIAL DIRECTOR or Sanction fit established Windows litigation-support teams. TrialView fits browser-centered or hybrid proceedings.


### Is there free trial presentation software?


Several specialist products in this shortlist offer a time-limited evaluation or free-trial route, including TrialPad, ExhibitView, Case Crafter, OnCue, and Sanction. Confirm current terms directly with each vendor. A PDF viewer and an existing slide application can handle a small, fully scripted matter, but they provide less control over ad hoc retrieval, synchronized testimony, presentation logs, and private output.


### What trial presentation software works on Mac?


TrialPad and Case Crafter run natively on Mac and iPad. TrialView is cloud-based and works across devices. OnCue, ExhibitView Trial Presenter, TRIAL DIRECTOR, and Sanction center on Windows, although ExhibitView also offers the separate iTrial iPad app.


### How much does TrialPad cost?


TrialPad is included in the $600-per-year LIT SUITE subscription rather than sold separately. The subscription includes five litigation apps, works across three compatible Apple devices, and starts with a seven-day trial.
